<reason>Both sides argued cleanly and followed the Q&A format properly, but CON built the more resilient mechanism-level case by round's end. CON's pivotal move was the "ex ante ordering uncertainty" argument (B4.2): a manager cannot know at order time which units will become disposal-bound surplus, so compliance risk pushes toward blanket under-ordering rather than trimming only wasteful margin. PRO's answer (A4.1-4.3) simply asserted the two streams "stay distinct" without explaining how a manager could sort future pantry-bound stock from future customer-bound stock at the moment of ordering, and PRO's closing never returned to rebuild that wall — CON's closing explicitly and accurately flagged this drop. CON also pressed a real asymmetry between voluntary tax-credit verification and mandatory per-item duty verification that PRO's "CON cannot call verification fatal here and essential there" line never fully answered. PRO's strongest moment was forcing CON to concede in A1 that stores remain legally free to trash food under an incentives-only regime, which PRO used effectively to frame CON's plan as tacitly preserving the status quo. That concession, however, was reframed by CON as a deliberate tradeoff for avoiding brittle enforcement and small-grocer harm, and PRO's closing answered that reframing with restated principle rather than fresh engagement. The debate is close and well-matched, but CON's unresolved mechanism argument gives it the cleaner path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's B4.2 ("compliance risk attaches at the moment of ordering, before that surplus even exists") answering PRO's A4.1-4.3 stream-distinction claim was the most decisive exchange — PRO never rebuilt the distinction in the closing, and CON's closing correctly called out that gap.</best_rebuttal>
